title: Haste Makes Waste? Towards Safe Few-Step Text-to-Image Models

paper.title: Haste Makes Waste? Towards Safe Few-Step Text-to-Image Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract While few-step distilled text-to-image models have gained traction due to their fast generation times, the speed-up implications on their unsafe generation rates remain unknown. We uncover an inherent tension between speed and safety: few-step models are often more unsafe than their teachers, and reducing the number of inference steps consistently raises unsafe generation rates. We further find that acceleration makes unsafe concepts harder to erase in few-step models, with existing concept-erasure methods markedly less effective than in teachers.
We offer a mechanistic diagnosis for why erasure methods fail on few-step models, finding that the fragility of few-step models’ generation process and the way generation guidance is usually distilled into those models may hinder established concept-erasure methods.
To address the speed-safety trade-off, we propose DICE ( Distillation-Integrated Concept Erasure ), a post-distillation erasure method tailored for few-step models. DICE aligns both its latent construction and its generation-preservation loss with the distillation method that produced the model, keeping erasure faithful to few-step models. DICE demonstrates strong results in our evaluation. For example, on FLUX Schnell, DICE reduces unsafe-generation rate to 0.046 (vs. ≥ \geq 0.161 for prior erasure method we test), while mostly preserving benign generation quality. 1 1 1 Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/plus-tau/safe-distilled-t2i .

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] are increasingly deployed in user-facing products, making the safety of the content they generate a first-order deployment concern. A dominant deployment trend over the past two years has been a move from many-step samplers to fast, distilled few-step variants—e.g., SD3.5 Turbo [ 2 , 5 ] , Sana Sprint [ 6 , 7 ] , FLUX Schnell [ 4 ] , and SCFM-style distilled models [ 8 ] —which generate images in one to four steps and are routinely shipped as drop-in replacements for their slower teachers. However, whether this acceleration preserves the safety properties of the underlying model has not been systematically audited. Prior work on T2I safety benchmarking [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] and on concept erasure (e.g., ESD [ 12 ] , UCE [ 13 ] , EraseAnything [ 14 ] , Meta-Unlearning [ 15 ] ) was developed and evaluated against full-step teacher models, and two questions of immediate deployment relevance remain open: (i) how does the safety profile of a T2I system change when it is shipped through the acceleration pipeline? and (ii) do existing concept-erasure defenses, applied at the natural insertion points of that pipeline, continue to function once the deployment target is a few-step distilled model? This paper sets to answer these questions. We find that acceleration is not safety-neutral—few-step acceleration and reducing T2I models’ inference step count both result in higher rates of unsafe content generation (§ III-B – III-C ). We then turn to checking whether existing concept-erasure methods originally designed for full-step baseline models are effective on few-step distilled models (§ III-D ). The results show that applying these to few-step models either directly (post-distillation), prior to distillation, or via transfer from the teacher is significantly less effective than applying them to full-step models. To better understand why erasure fails in few-step models, we carry a mechanistic study (§ IV ). A simple explanation would be that acceleration and concept erasure directly compete. However, we find that the update directions of acceleration and erasure techniques are mostly orthogonal, suggesting that other issues hinder erasure within few-step models. Complementing prior work on the geometry and early decision concentration of few-step models [ 16 , 17 ] , our empirical analyses uncover two failure modes that emerge when full-step teachers are distilled into one-to-four-step students. First, few-step students are more brittle under small changes: relative to their teachers, perturbing either the latent input or the model weights slightly can drastically change the student’s next generation update. Second, the way guidance is baked into the weights of few-step models distorts the concept direction used during erasure: the student direction is rotated away from the teacher’s and inflated in norm, driving erasure updates to a degraded target. Together, these findings suggest that existing erasure methods fail not because safety and speed are inherently incompatible, but because post-hoc edits are applied to models whose few-step generation behavior differs from the full-step models those methods were designed for. In an attempt to address the gap, we present DICE ( Distillation-Integrated Concept Erasure )—to our knowledge, the first concept-erasure method tailored for few-step models. DICE retargets two key components of the standard erasure so they are better fit for the distilled student: (i) the generation-preservation loss keeps the edited model’s output close to the original distilled model’s, rather than the standard flow-matching training target that acceleration methods may deviate from; and (ii) the noisy latent on which the ESD loss is evaluated is sampled along the straight noise-to-image line between Gaussian noise and a clean concept image generated by the frozen student—mirroring the latent construction used in distillation rather than the deployment scheduler grid where erasure direction may be degraded and where the few-step model is sensitive to minor perturbations. We instantiate DICE on FLUX Schnell, SD3.5 Turbo and FLUX SCFM, evaluate it on safety, speed, and quality axes, and run ablations that isolate the two design choices. Across the methods we evaluate, DICE is the only configuration that simultaneously significantly reduces unsafe concept generation (pixel-level detectors and Unsafe@k, with qualitative confirmation) and maintains general image quality on already-distilled rectified-flow models. We summarize our core contributions as follows: • We show that T2I acceleration is not safety-neutral: a trade-off exists between safety and speed in current open-weights flow-matching models (§ III-B – III-C ). • We show that current concept-erasure methods do not effectively erase unsafe concepts from few-step models (§ III-D ); our mechanistic study helps shed light on why these methods may fail (§ IV ). • Motivated by our findings, we present DICE, an erasure method tailored for few-step models that is able to better suppress unsafe concepts while preserving image quality in these models (§ V ).

sections.heading: II-A Flow-Matching T2I Models
sections.text: Recent T2I models increasingly adopt flow-matching or rectified-flow formulations. These models operate in the latent space of a pretrained Variational Autoencoder (VAE). They learn a velocity field that defines a generative path from a noise sample x 1 x_{1} to a clean image latent x 0 x_{0} , and generation is performed by numerically integrating this learned velocity field. A solver timestep t t indexes a noise level σ t \sigma_{t} from the model’s noise schedule, with σ t ≈ 1 \sigma_{t}\approx 1 near the noisy endpoint and σ t ≈ 0 \sigma_{t}\approx 0 near the clean endpoint. For a text condition c c and model parameters θ \theta , we write the predicted velocity as v θ ​ ( z t , c , t ) v_{\theta}(z_{t},c,t) . The corresponding noisy latent can be written as the linear interpolation z t = ( 1 − σ t ) ​ x 0 + σ t ​ x 1 = x 0 + σ t ​ ( x 1 − x 0 ) z_{t}=(1-\sigma_{t})x_{0}+\sigma_{t}x_{1}=x_{0}+\sigma_{t}(x_{1}-x_{0}) (1) where x 1 x_{1} is Gaussian noise. The learned velocity field specifies how to move along this path during sampling. Starting from noise z t = 1 = x 1 z_{t=1}=x_{1} , the sampler repeatedly evaluates v θ ​ ( z t , c , t ) v_{\theta}(z_{t},c,t) and takes numerical integration steps toward lower noise levels, producing an estimate of the clean latent at t = 0 t=0 . During flow-matching training, the model is supervised to predict the reverse denoising velocity of the interpolation in Eq. 1 : since ∂ z t / ∂ σ t = x 1 − x 0 \partial z_{t}/\partial\sigma_{t}=x_{1}-x_{0} , the target direction for decreasing noise is x 1 − x 0 x_{1}-x_{0} . Thus the denoiser learns the direction that transports noisy latents back toward clean image latents, which are then decoded to images using the VAE decoder. When the endpoints and timestep are clear from context, we write a noisy latent simply as z z , omitting the particular x 0 x_{0} , x 1 x_{1} , and t t used to construct it. We use this notation to distinguish two ways of obtaining latents z z for analysis or erasure training. When z z is synthetic and obtained by running a particular model for one or more solver steps along its own sampling trajectory, we call it on-policy for that model. When z z is constructed outside that rollout, by taking a clean image x 0 x_{0} and re-noising it to a chosen σ t \sigma_{t} using Eq. 1 , we call it off-policy . Compared to classical DDPM/DDIM-style [ 18 ] diffusion sampling, rectified-flow formulations are designed to support straighter trajectories and fewer integration steps. However, these models still commonly require many solver steps at inference. Two prominent open examples are FLUX Dev and SD3.5 Large [ 19 , 2 ] . SD3.5 Large uses standard classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 20 ] : the model is evaluated with both the text condition c c and the null condition ∅ \varnothing , and the guided velocity is formed as v CFG ​ ( z , c , t , ω ) = v θ ​ ( z , ∅ , t ) + ω ⁡ ( v θ ​ ( z , c , t ) − v θ ​ ( z , ∅ , t ) ) , v_{\mathrm{CFG}}(z,c,t;\omega)=v_{\theta}(z,\varnothing,t)+\omega\left(v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-v_{\theta}(z,\varnothing,t)\right), where ω \omega is the guidance scale. This keeps the guidance operation external to the model weights and preserves separate conditional and unconditional predictions at inference. FLUX Dev handles guidance differently: it conditions the model on a guidance scalar and approximates guided generation in a single forward pass: v CFG ​ ( z , c , t , ω ) = v θ ​ ( z , c , t , ω ) v_{\mathrm{CFG}}(z,c,t;\omega)=v_{\theta}(z,c,t,\omega) We refer to this as guidance distillation, and distinguish it from few-step distillation. Guidance distillation changes how CFG is represented, while few-step distillation changes the number and size of solver steps the model is trained to support. FLUX Dev is guidance-distilled from the closed-weights FLUX Pro, but it is not a few-step model, and is sampled with many inference steps, 50 by default.

sections.heading: II-B Few-Step Models
sections.text: To accelerate generation, few-step distillation trains a student model to generate high-quality images in only 1–4 inference steps. In many modern T2I settings, the student shares the teacher architecture and is initialized from the teacher, but its training objective differs from the original flow-matching objective: instead of learning only the local velocity target used to train the teacher, the student is optimized to reproduce the teacher’s behavior under much larger sampling steps. Distillation methods We study several forms of few-step distillation. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (ADD) combines teacher-based distillation with an adversarial objective, encouraging the student to produce realistic samples in the aggressive 1–4 step regime. Latent Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (LADD) performs adversarial distillation in the latent space of a pretrained latent diffusion model, using synthetic teacher-generated data. In T2I applications, ADD/LADD students are trained to match a guided teacher and are then sampled without external CFG. We refer to this as guidance “bake-in,” as the CFG behavior is baked into the student’s weights. As a result, a particular teacher-guidance regime is effectively absorbed into the student. Shortcut Consistency Flow Matching (SCFM), by contrast, is a consistency-based method for flow-matching models. It builds shortcut targets by composing two smaller velocity steps over a longer interval. The objective contains both a teacher-guided term, where the two-step target is computed using the frozen pretrained flow model, and a self-distillation term, where the target is computed using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) or online student. Thus, the frozen teacher remains a fixed anchor throughout training, while the EMA term encourages internal shortcut consistency. In this sense, SCFM is a lighter, progressive-like form of acceleration: the original SCFM work targets moderate few-step sampling in the 3–8 step regime with substantially less training time than ADD/LADD-style distillation, while staying closer to the teacher’s velocity-space objective. This variety is important for our work. SD3.5 Turbo is described as an adversarially distilled variant of SD3.5 Large, trained using ADD [ 2 ] . FLUX Schnell is publicly described as a few-step model trained using LADD, but the specific teacher model and full distillation recipe are not disclosed [ 21 , 19 ] . Thus, unlike SD3.5 Turbo, FLUX Schnell does not provide a known teacher-student pair for controlled analysis. We therefore apply SCFM to FLUX Dev to obtain FLUX SCFM, a controlled FLUX-based teacher-student pair with a known teacher. Overall, we evaluate released few-step checkpoints together with FLUX SCFM, covering adversarial, latent-adversarial, and consistency/shortcut distillation.

sections.heading: II-C Concept Erasure
sections.text: Concept erasure aims to remove an undesirable concept from a pretrained T2I model while preserving its ability to generate unrelated content. Erased concepts may correspond to unsafe content, copyrighted styles, memorized identities, or other concepts that a model provider wants to suppress. A prominent family of erasure methods fine-tunes the model by optimizing gradient-based objectives. A central building block in this family is the ESD loss, introduced by Erased Stable Diffusion (ESD) and reused by many later fine-tuning-based erasure methods [ 12 , 15 , 14 , 11 , 22 , 23 ] . ℒ ESD \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESD}} suppresses a target concept by modifying the model’s conditional prediction relative to its unconditional prediction. In velocity-prediction notation, it can be written as ℒ ESD = \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESD}}={} ∥ v θ ( z , c , t ) − [ v θ ⋆ ( z , ∅ , t ) \displaystyle\Bigl\|v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-\Bigl[v_{\theta^{\star}}(z,\varnothing,t) (2) − η ( v θ ⋆ ( z , c , t ) − v θ ⋆ ( z , ∅ , t ) ) ] ∥ 2 2 \displaystyle-\eta\bigl(v_{\theta^{\star}}(z,c,t)-v_{\theta^{\star}}(z,\varnothing,t)\bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr\|_{2}^{2} where v θ ⋆ v_{\theta^{\star}} is the frozen pretrained model, v θ v_{\theta} is the edited model, c c is the erased concept, ∅ \varnothing is the null condition, and the negative guidance strength η \eta controls the strength of the negative signal. Intuitively, the method pushes the edited model away from the concept direction encoded by the difference between conditional and unconditional predictions. Recent methods for fine-tuning T2I models have adopted Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 24 ] . Instead of updating the full weight matrix ( θ ℓ \theta_{\ell} ) of each layer ( ℓ \ell ), LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and learns a low-rank residual update, θ ℓ ← θ ℓ + Δ ​ θ ℓ , Δ ​ θ ℓ = B ℓ ​ A ℓ , \theta_{\ell}\leftarrow\theta_{\ell}+\Delta\theta_{\ell},\qquad\Delta\theta_{\ell}=B_{\ell}A_{\ell}, (3) where A ℓ ∈ ℝ r × d in A_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} and B ℓ ∈ ℝ d out × r B_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r} are trainable low-rank matrices, with r ≪ min ⁡ ( d in , d out ) r\ll\min(d_{\mathrm{in}},d_{\mathrm{out}}) . This parameterization has become popular due to its simplicity and effectiveness, as well as its ability to substantially reduce the number of optimized parameters, enabling faster and more memory-efficient training. Since the original model weights remain fixed and only the residual update ( Δ ​ θ ℓ \Delta\theta_{\ell} ) is optimized, LoRA can also help preserve the pretrained model and mitigate catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning. Not all erasure methods are fine-tuning-based. We also include UCE [ 13 ] and SPEED [ 25 ] as closed-form editing methods. UCE analytically edits the model’s text-conditioning projections in order to modify how specific text concepts are mapped into the image-generation process, without iterative fine-tuning. SPEED refines UCE to enable multiple concept erasure and precise edits specific to target concepts. In older U-Net-based [ 26 ] diffusion models these edits target cross-attention projections; in transformer-based models such as FLUX and SD3.5, the corresponding edits apply to the initial text-conditioning projection layers rather than to cross-attention modules. Most concept-erasure methods were designed and evaluated primarily on SD 1.x-style latent diffusion models with U-Net backbones, DDPM/DDIM-style denoising objectives, and standard CFG sampling. Their assumptions do not necessarily transfer cleanly to modern T2I models such as FLUX and SD3.5, which use Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) [ 27 ] backbones and flow-matching velocity prediction rather than DDPM/DDIM-style noise prediction. A recent work, EraseAnything, explicitly targets concept erasure in newer flow-matching T2I models and shows that adapting erasure to these architectures requires additional care [ 14 ] . We therefore evaluate both classical erasure methods and EraseAnything.

sections.heading: II-D Threat Model
sections.text: We consider a defender that modifies a pretrained, potentially distilled T2I model to prevent the generation of prohibited visual content while preserving its benign generation quality and inference speed. In line with prior work (e.g., [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] ), we primarily assume a black-box adversary who controls input prompts and seeks to elicit prohibited content. In evaluations of adaptive adversaries (§ V-C ), we further consider adversaries with white-box access to the text encoder and to the full model weights.

sections.heading: III Empirical Safety Trade-offs
sections.text: We begin by exploring the safety implications of few-step acceleration, contrasting few-step students with full-step teacher models (§ III-B ), and assessing how reducing the number of generation steps impacts safety (§ III-C ). Our results show a consistent trade-off between speed and safety: faster generation (i.e., lower number of generation steps) is associated with more unsafe content emitted by the models. We also apply popular and leading erasure methods [ 12 , 14 , 13 ] to few-step models and check their impact on safety, speed, and utility (§ III-D ). We find that erasure methods demonstrate significantly lower efficacy over all the few-step models we test. We further test alternative strategies to integrate few-step acceleration and erasures, such as erasing a teacher before distillation (§ III-D ). Across all strategies, erasure remains consistently weaker in the resulting few-step models than in their full-step counterparts, while introducing additional strategy-specific weaknesses. Before describing our findings, we present the experimental setup (§ III-A ).

sections.heading: III-A Experimental Setup
sections.text: Models For our experiments, we focus on rectified flow-matching models, which have emerged as a dominant formulation in recent state-of-the-art T2I systems [ 27 ] , specifically the popular FLUX and SD3.5 model families. Both have few-step variants produced using ADD/LADD [ 5 , 7 ] —SD3.5 Turbo which is based on SD3.5 Large [ 2 ] , and FLUX Schnell which is produced using LADD [ 7 , 4 ] , but the specific teacher model used is not disclosed. Thus, we employ the SCFM distillation method [ 8 ] over FLUX Dev to produce FLUX SCFM. We use the SCFM training recipe and parameters recommended by Cai et al. [ 8 ] —full details are in App. A-A . By training FLUX SCFM, we effectively create a known teacher-student pair for the FLUX model family. Because SCFM is a distillation method based on the self-consistency loss [ 28 ] rather than an adversarial-based loss like ADD or LADD, FLUX SCFM helps us corroborate our findings on a profoundly different distillation approach. Since few-step distillation is a resource-intensive process compared to concept erasure or inference, and since we already have a known open-weights student-teacher pair in the SD3.5 family, we do not apply SCFM training for the SD3.5 family. Another approach for producing a student for FLUX would be applying LADD ourselves, but the LADD process is significantly more resource intensive [ 8 ] than SCFM, making it infeasible to run. We use each model through its official implementation in the diffusers library, together with default components it supplies: the Euler Discrete scheduler and its timestep schedule, the image variational autoencoder (VAE), and the corresponding text tokenizer and encoder. Unless stated otherwise, we use the recommended default inference configuration for each model [ 4 , 8 , 2 ] : CFG scale 3.5 for SD3.5 and FLUX, CFG scale 5 for FLUX SCFM, which lies within its recommended operating range [4.5, 6], 28 inference steps for SD3.5 Large, 50 inference steps for FLUX Dev, and 4 inference steps for all few-step models. Unsafe prompts and safety checkers Following common practice [ 29 , 9 , 12 ] , we assess nudity and violence erasure, with nudity being our main focus. Due to a lack of explicitness we encounter in the widely used I2P [ 9 ] dataset, we follow multiple recent papers [ 30 , 31 ] and use the NSFW-56k [ 10 ] dataset for nudity, which we find significantly more explicit. We report results on a randomly selected subset of 1k prompts from the NSFW-56k dataset (hereafter, NSFW-1k). We also report results on the I2P dataset, adopted due to its popularity in the field [ 12 , 14 , 23 ] in App. B-G . To evaluate the safety of generated images in the nudity use-case, we leverage two widely used detectors: NudeNet [ 32 ] , a CNN-based detector, and SD-Checker [ 33 ] , a CLIP-based detector shipped with earlier Stable Diffusion releases. We find the two checkers to be mutually consistent, and both have been shown to agree with human annotators [ 34 ] . App. B-F describes the evaluation of violence erasure, yielding results consistent with those of nudity erasure. Metrics Both detectors yield a per-image binary unsafe label, and we report their mean unsafe detection rate, i.e., the fraction of generated images flagged as unsafe. NudeNet outputs a set of detected body-part boxes each with a confidence score. We use its default detection threshold 0.2 and label an image as unsafe if it contains at least one detection from a fixed set of explicit-nudity classes (App. A-B ). SD-Checker directly returns a binary unsafe flag, which we use as-is. Since few-step distilled models may reduce diversity [ 17 ] , we also report results over new metrics we introduce—the NudeNet@k and SD-Checker@k metrics—we generate k k different images using different noise seeds for each prompt, and we categorize the generation instance as unsafe if any of the k k images is deemed unsafe by the baseline safety checker (throughout the paper, we use k k =5). Intuitively, NudeNet@k and SD-Checker@k better reflect realistic adversary capabilities in practice, as they can probe T2I models multiple times until unsafe content is generated. To measure the overall benign generation quality of a model, we use the HPSv2 benchmark [ 35 ] . We prefer HPSv2 as opposed to the FID score [ 36 ] because it is prompt-conditioned, trained on large-scale human preference annotations, and is arguably more fit to the evaluation of T2I models [ 37 ] . That said, due to the widespread use of FID for measuring distributional alignment and CLIP-based image-text similarity for measuring prompt adherence [ 38 ] , we also report these metrics on COCO-30k [ 39 ] in App. B-H . Erasure methods We evaluate two fine-tuning-based erasure methods and one closed-form edit-based method, chosen to cover influential representatives of the dominant practical erasure paradigms. ESD [ 12 ] is a foundational and widely adopted fine-tuning-based method in the erasure literature. EraseAnything [ 14 ] is a recent LoRA-based [ 24 ] erasure method tailored for flow-matching models, making it especially relevant for modern models such as FLUX Dev. Finally, UCE [ 13 ] is widely used due to its simplicity and closed-form update, and we include it as a representative edit-based alternative to fine-tuning-based erasure. Out of the erasure methods we test, ESD and UCE were designed for older U-Net-style models, and none were designed for few-step models. To adapt them to the tested models, we perform a grid search over their negative guidance and learning rate parameters, selecting the configuration that maximally erases unsafe content while best preserving benign generation quality.

We begin by examining the unsafe generation rates of out-of-the-box few-step and full-step models. Tab. I reports the unsafe generation rates of each few-step student alongside its full-step teacher. Across both model families and all four safety metrics, the few-step student is consistently less safe than its teacher. The SD3.5 Turbo student raises the NudeNet rate from 0.2432 to 0.3232 (a 33% relative increase) and the SD-Checker rate from 0.5416 to 0.6646 relative to SD3.5 Large; analogously, FLUX SCFM raises the NudeNet rate from 0.2562 to 0.3282 and the SD-Checker rate from 0.6108 to 0.7074 relative to FLUX Dev. The gap persists under the Unsafe@k metrics, where a prompt is flagged unsafe if any of its k k =5 seeds is flagged: this shows that acceleration not only increases the average unsafe rate but also makes at least one unsafe generation more likely under repeated sampling. Taken together, these consistent gaps suggest that few-step distillation can systematically erode the implicit safety behavior inherited from the teacher. FLUX Schnell is marginally safer than FLUX Dev (e.g. 0.2348 vs. 0.2562 on NudeNet) and may seem to contradict our conclusion at first glance. However, as discussed in § II-B , the teacher of FLUX Schnell is not publicly disclosed and is not necessarily FLUX Dev (itself a guidance-distilled variant of the closed-weights FLUX Pro). This is therefore not a clean teacher-student comparison, thus we exclude FLUX Schnell from Tab. I . Beyond binary flag rates, we exploit the internal mechanism of the SD-Checker to derive a continuous unsafety score. Internally, the SD-Checker embeds an image with CLIP and measures its cosine similarity to a fixed collection of unsafe-concept embeddings, flagging the image as unsafe whenever its similarity to any concept exceeds a per-concept threshold [ 33 ] . We define the SD-Checker severity of an image as the maximal cosine similarity between its CLIP embedding and any unsafe concept in this collection. Fig. 1 shows the severity distribution, displayed as a continuous measure of unsafe content instead of a binary prediction. The student’s distribution is shifted toward higher severity values, and the effect is most pronounced in the upper tail: 77% of the images with a severity above 0.25 are produced by the SD3.5 Turbo few-step student.

sections.heading: III-C Step Count Is a Hidden Safety Knob
sections.text: Following § III-B ’s findings, we try to further understand why few-step models generate more unsafe content. To this end, we check the model unsafe generation rates by the number of inference steps used. We discover that the number of steps taken impacts the generation safety metrics. We conduct an experiment where we generate 200 images per model and step count, making sure to re-use the same noise seeds for all configurations, so that the results of a given model across different step counts would be directly comparable. We condition the models on the prompt “A photo of a gorgeous woman, erotic”, and measure the cosine similarity in CLIP’s embedding space between the generated image and the “nudity” concept. In Fig. 2 , we show the cosine similarity by step count for the baseline models—there is an evident trend of decreased similarity with “nudity” as the number of steps increases, both for few-step and full-step models. Concretely, lowering the step count raises the mean CLIP similarity to “nudity” by up to ∼ \sim 9% for full-step models (FLUX Dev, 0.239 to 0.261 going from 50 to 8 steps) and up to ∼ \sim 7% for few-step models (SD3.5 Turbo, 0.231 to 0.248 going from 8 to 1 step). sections.heading: III-D Integrating Erasure With Few-Step Models
sections.text: We now assess three intuitive means for integrating erasure with few-step acceleration at three different points. In pre-distillation erasure , the teacher is erased first and the erased teacher is then distilled into a few-step student. In post-distillation erasure , the erasure method is applied directly to an already-distilled few-step checkpoint. In Teacher-LoRA transfer [ 17 ] , an erasure LoRA trained on the teacher is loaded onto the student. These choices differ in practicality: pre-distillation erasure requires teacher access and an expensive distillation run for each erased concept; Teacher-LoRA transfer requires teacher access, a shared teacher-student architecture, and a LoRA-based erasure method. Post-distillation erasure is the most easily deployable because it only requires the released few-step model; we therefore first evaluate it. In Tab. III , we apply existing erasure methods directly to few-step models and compare them with the same methods applied to their full-step counterparts. The trend is consistent across methods and metrics: post-distillation erasure leaves substantially higher unsafe generation rates on few-step students. sections.heading: IV Mechanistic Diagnosis of Erasure’s Failure
sections.text: We investigate three candidate explanations for why erasure fails on few-step models. We first rule out the most obvious one—a direct conflict between the speed and erasure objectives (§ IV-A ). We then identify two mechanisms connected to erasure’s failure: aggressively distilled models are geometrically fragile, amplifying any perturbation to their weights or latents (§ IV-B ), and the concept direction that fine-tuning-based erasure relies on is degraded by how guidance is handled during distillation (§ IV-C ).

sections.heading: IV-A Non-Conflicting Speed and Erasure Objectives
sections.text: We set out to determine whether there is an inherent conflict between the few-step objective and the erasure objective. Because LADD distillation is resource-heavy and time-consuming, we focus on SCFM distillation. For the erasure objective we adopt the ESD loss, owing to its popularity and simplicity and because it forms the erasure term in many fine-tuning-based erasure methods [ 12 , 15 , 14 , 11 , 22 , 23 ] . We compute the ESD gradients with respect to the same Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 24 ] adapter parameters SCFM optimizes in every layer ℓ \ell : A ℓ , B ℓ A_{\ell},B_{\ell} (Eq. 3 ). The tuned layers match those used in the SCFM method [ 8 ] and cover both the attention and feed-forward layers of the transformer blocks. We run the initial phase of SCFM distillation training on both SD3.5 Large and FLUX Dev. We compute the ESD gradient as in Eq. 2 with respect to the LoRA parameters A ℓ , B ℓ A_{\ell},B_{\ell} of every attention and feed-forward layer ℓ \ell (and analogously for the SCFM gradient at the same iteration), without taking an optimization step in the ESD direction. The ESD gradients are computed over a set of 50 images sampled from the base model, using the “nudity” concept—the original concept used by the ESD method. For each pair of SCFM and ESD gradients, we use the same noise level σ t \sigma_{t} . The ESD gradients are computed every 8 steps over the first 20k images, which constitute the initial 12.5% iterations of SCFM distillation. Restricting the analysis to this early window, prior to convergence, keeps the model close to the base model, where the erasure and acceleration gradients are strongest. Following prior work in multi-task and multi-objective optimization [ 40 , 41 ] , we quantify objective conflict by measuring the cosine similarity between the gradients induced by the two losses on the shared trainable parameters. We compute the cosine similarity between the ESD and SCFM gradients and group the cosine-similarity values into three noise-level bins with equal size: early, mid, and late. We report the mean and standard deviation of these values per bin in Tab. IV . sections.heading: IV-C Distillation Degrades the Erasure-Gradient Direction
sections.text: Degradation hypothesis We hypothesize that guidance distillation in few-step models degrades the erasure direction. Fine-tuning-based erasure suppresses a concept by regressing the conditional prediction along − δ -\delta , where the concept direction δ \delta is defined in Eq. 7 . We also define the respective full-step reference concept axis δ ∗ \delta^{*} for the full-step model v ∗ v^{*} : δ = v ⁡ ( z , c ) − v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) , δ ∗ = v ∗ ​ ( z , c ) − v ∗ ​ ( z , ∅ ) \delta=v(z,c)-v(z,\varnothing),\qquad\delta^{*}=v^{*}(z,c)-v^{*}(z,\varnothing) (7) In our diagnosis, we focus on the ESD loss because it is the main erasure term used in the loss of many fine-tuning-based erasure methods [ 12 , 15 , 14 , 11 , 22 , 23 ] . Concretely, ESD fine-tunes the model so that its concept prediction v ⁡ ( z , c ) v(z,c) matches, under an MSE loss, the CFG-agnostic target v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) − η ⁡ ( v ⁡ ( z , c ) − v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) ) v(z,\varnothing)-\eta(v(z,c)-v(z,\varnothing)) , where η \eta is a negative guidance scale hyperparameter. The ESD target is computed from a frozen copy of the same model, for latents z z sampled along the model’s own trajectory, generated using the concept prompt conditioning (described below); near initialization, this is equivalent to pushing the prediction along − δ -\delta , away from the concept (App. B-C ). Since erasure is usually a short fine-tuning process of only ∼ 100 {\sim}100 – 200 200 iterations, the edited model remains close to this frozen copy for most of optimization, making this approximation useful. The conditioned branch v ⁡ ( z , c ) v(z,c) is directly reshaped by distillation. Few-step models with baked-in guidance such as SD3.5 Turbo and FLUX Schnell are trained to reproduce CFG sampling in a single forward pass, without an explicit guidance step; their conditional branch therefore bakes in classifier-free guidance, so v ⁡ ( z , c ) v(z,c) approximates the CFG-combined full-step reference rather than the raw teacher velocity: v ⁡ ( z , c ) ≈ v ∗ ​ ( z , ∅ ) + ω ⁡ ( v ∗ ​ ( z , c ) − v ∗ ​ ( z , ∅ ) ) v ⁡ ( z , c ) ≉ v ∗ ​ ( z , c ) . \begin{gathered}v(z,c)\approx v^{*}(z,\varnothing)+\omega(v^{*}(z,c)-v^{*}(z,\varnothing))\\ v(z,c)\not\approx v^{*}(z,c).\end{gathered} (The exact ω \omega used during the distillation process of SD3.5 Turbo and FLUX Schnell is undisclosed.) The unconditioned branch is also altered by distillation, but in a different way than the conditioned branch. The unconditioned branch v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) v(z,\varnothing) is never directly trained in LADD or SCFM distillations, making it unclear how its velocity trajectory changes compared to the baseline model. At the same time, v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) v(z,\varnothing) shares all the parameters θ \theta with the tuned conditioned path v ⁡ ( z , c ) v(z,c) , so it is still reshaped indirectly as those shared parameters are updated. Because the conditioned branch v ⁡ ( z , c ) v(z,c) and the unconditioned branch v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) v(z,\varnothing) that form δ \delta are reshaped by distillation in different ways, unlike standard full-step T2I model training where both are optimized together, the erasure direction may be degraded with irrelevant information. Compensating for this degradation analytically is impractical, since the student’s branches do not exactly reproduce the full-step baseline’s ( v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) ≉ v ∗ ​ ( z , ∅ ) v(z,\varnothing)\not\approx v^{*}(z,\varnothing) ) and the distillation-time ω \omega is usually undisclosed. Consequently, as we show next, erasure receives a direction that points in a different direction than the full-step reference’s and is substantially larger in magnitude. Measuring the concept-direction degradation To put the hypothesis to the test, we compute δ \delta and δ ∗ \delta^{*} (Eq. 7 ), and measure the Frobenius norm of both and the cosine similarity between them using matching seeds. If the ESD direction is indeed degraded in few-step models, we expect to see low similarity between them, and a distorted magnitude | ‖ δ ‖ − ‖ δ ∗ ‖ | ≫ 0 |\|\delta\|-\|\delta^{*}\||\gg 0 . We draw 1,000 image-timestep pairs—a sample size that supplies us with a large enough standard deviation number to draw meaningful conclusions and is small enough to run efficiently. Using synthetic images may bias the results in the direction of the model which generated them—so we use real images from LAION-Pop. Each image-timestep pair samples a LAION-Pop image latent x 0 x_{0} , draws σ t \sigma_{t} uniformly in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , and forms the off-policy latent z = ( 1 − σ t ) ​ x 0 + σ t ​ ϵ z=(1-\sigma_{t})\,x_{0}+\sigma_{t}\,\epsilon , so the latents are not drawn from any single model’s own generative distribution. On each z z we evaluate the concept direction δ = v ⁡ ( z , c ) − v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) \delta=v(z,c)-v(z,\varnothing) for every model (FLUX Dev, FLUX Schnell, FLUX SCFM, SD3.5 Large and SD3.5 Turbo), with c c =“nudity”, the concept originally used in the ESD method. For the aggressively-distilled few-step variants, each variant’s concept direction δ \delta points in a markedly different direction compared to its in-family full-step reference δ ∗ \delta^{*} . The average cosine similarity between the two is only 0.30 0.30 for SD3.5 Turbo (against its SD3.5 Large reference) and 0.07 0.07 for FLUX Schnell (against FLUX Dev). For few-step models, the erasure direction is also larger in magnitude, by ≈ {\approx} 1.2–3.9 × \times for SD3.5 Turbo and ≈ {\approx} 2–5 × \times for FLUX Schnell (against FLUX Dev), with the absolute gap widest at high-noise timesteps (Fig. 5 ). This implies that the velocities v ⁡ ( z , c ) v(z,c) and v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) v(z,\varnothing) are significantly closer to each other in the full-step model than in the few-step variant, degrading the erasure objective of the student. This holds even though all four velocities ‖ v ⁡ ( z , c ) ‖ , ‖ v ⁡ ( z , ∅ ) ‖ , ‖ v ∗ ​ ( z , c ) ‖ \|v(z,c)\|,\|v(z,\varnothing)\|,\|v^{*}(z,c)\| and ‖ v ∗ ​ ( z , ∅ ) ‖ \|v^{*}(z,\varnothing)\| have similar norms (App. B-D ). In other words, the inflation reflects poorer cancellation, not larger predictions. The lightly distilled FLUX SCFM follows this trend only weakly: its δ \delta stays positively aligned with FLUX Dev’s ( cos = 0.64 \cos=0.64 ) and is only ∼ 1.4 × {\sim}1.4\times larger in magnitude, far milder than the aggressively distilled variants above, consistent with its lighter distillation. The effect is strongest in high noise regions where σ t ∼ 1 \sigma_{t}\sim 1 The largest absolute distortion in δ \delta occurs where few-step erasure methods are most likely to sample their training-time latents ( z z ) from: Existing fine-tuning-based erasure methods typically sample z z on-policy from the model’s own denoising trajectory; for aggressive few-step σ t \sigma_{t} schedules, especially one-step schedules, those samples are naturally concentrated near high-noise timesteps even without an explicit timestep shift in the scheduler. Thus, the degraded ESD direction is not merely present in few-step models: it is emphasized by the sampling distribution used during erasure, motivating the sampling strategy we use in § V . Guidance bake-in contributes to erasure direction degradation Unlike models that apply CFG externally (e.g., SD3.5 Large) and have guidance-agnostic per-pass velocities, FLUX Dev and FLUX SCFM take the classifier-free-guidance scale as an explicit network input, letting us vary it to isolate its effect on δ \delta . Raising CFG on FLUX Dev from 1.0 to 3.5 inflates ‖ δ ‖ \|\delta\| about 3.6 × \times (17.8 → \to 64.1) and nudges its cosine with FLUX Schnell’s δ \delta upward (0.055 → \to 0.068); on FLUX SCFM the same sweep grows ‖ δ ‖ \|\delta\| from 18.6 (CFG of 1.0) to 90.2 (CFG of 5.0), with FLUX Dev and FLUX SCFM near-identical at matched CFG. These results show that increasing guidance alone reproduces the δ \delta -inflation seen in few-step models, suggesting guidance bake-in as a direct cause for the erasure degradation. A natural remedy follows from the sweep above: since baked-in extra guidance is a large contributor to the inflation of δ \delta , one could run the erasure itself using ω = 1 \omega=1 , effectively disabling CFG (Eq. 2 ). This is only possible for models that expose the guidance scale as an explicit input (i.e. not applicable for FLUX Schnell nor SD3.5 Turbo). We discuss this in more detail in App. B-E . Taken together, these results show that the ESD concept direction δ \delta in few-step models is a degraded erasure target: it is rotated away from the full-step model direction and inflated in magnitude. The CFG sweep identifies guidance bake-in as a main driver: folding classifier-free guidance into the conditional velocity degrades δ \delta , and higher effective guidance inflates it further. This distortion is strongest at high noise inputs, directly motivating the sampling changes in § V . Even the lightly-distilled FLUX SCFM shows a milder version of this effect at its higher operational CFG scale.

sections.heading: V Concept Erasure for Few-Step Models
sections.text: We set out to design a robust concept erasure method for few-step T2I models. Across the different erasure integration points, we choose post-distillation erasure as (i) the teacher model does not need to be accessible or even known (e.g., FLUX Schnell); and (ii) the costly distillation process does not need to be modified or re-run for every erased concept. Given those benefits, our method must overcome the empirical struggles of post-distillation erasure: it should suppress the target concept while preserving the few-step model’s benign generation quality. Our method addresses the two failure modes identified in § IV : it avoids over-training on the high-noise latents where few-step models are most fragile and where the ESD concept direction is most degraded, and it constrains the edited model to stay close to the frozen pre-erasure few-step velocity field. Toward attaining these objectives, we design D istillation- I ntegrated C oncept E rasure ( DICE ) as a fine-tuning-based LoRA-based method, keeping erasure modular and inexpensive. DICE targets the weights of the joint-attention layers in both text and image streams of the MMDiT architecture used in SD3.5 and FLUX, where concept-bearing text tokens interact with image tokens. DICE objective Let θ ∗ \theta^{*} denote the frozen pre-erasure few-step model, and let θ \theta denote the edited model obtained by training LoRA adapters on top of it while keeping the base weights fixed. DICE optimizes a fixed weighted sum of three losses: ℒ DICE ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 c , t , z ​ [ ℒ esd + λ 1 ​ ℒ attn + λ 2 ​ ℒ gen ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DICE}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{c,t,z}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{esd}}+\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{attn}}+\lambda_{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}\right], (8) where c c is the erased concept prompt and t t is the sampled noise level. The ESD term keeps the concept-suppression target used by many gradient-based erasure methods (Eq. 2 ). At first glance, continuing to use an ESD-style term may seem counterintuitive after § IV-C , where we show that the ESD concept direction is degraded in few-step models. However, § IV-A suggests that the speed and erasure update directions are not inherently contradictory. DICE keeps the useful concept-suppression direction, but changes the conditions under which it is optimized: by controlling the latent distribution (§ V-A ), and preventing destructive drift away from the distilled model (§ V-B ). We additionally adopt the attention-map suppression loss ℒ attn \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{attn}} introduced by EraseAnything [ 14 ] to directly suppress the model’s internal use of the erased concept token. In the joint-attention blocks of the MMDiT, the text and image tokens are concatenated into a single sequence over which a softmax QK attention map assigns every (text or image) query token a distribution of attention weights across all key tokens. The key columns indexed by the erased concept’s tokenized positions therefore measure how strongly each query token attends to the concept, i.e., how much the concept token feeds the model’s internal representation. Following EraseAnything, ℒ attn \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{attn}} is computed from the attention map produced for the concept prompt c c : it restricts the map to concept key (e.g., “nude”) tokens and accumulates their magnitude into a single scalar that grows with the attention mass routed into the erased concept key text tokens. Minimizing ℒ attn \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{attn}} suppresses concept-specific activation inside the transformer rather than only changing the final velocity prediction, and helps us overcome the degraded erasure direction (§ IV-C ) better, as a secondary erasure loss not dependent on ESD. The generation term prevents the edited model’s velocity field from diverging too far from the pre-erasure model’s velocity field: ℒ gen = ‖ v θ ​ ( z , c , t ) − v θ ∗ ​ ( z , c , t ) ‖ 2 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}}=\left\|v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-v_{\theta^{*}}(z,c,t)\right\|_{2}^{2} (9) We optimize Eq. 8 with standard stochastic first-order updates, using AdamW as the optimizer. Each iteration samples a timestep/noise level and builds the inputs for the three loss terms. In all experiments, DICE targets the query, key, value, and output projections of the joint-attention blocks. Technical details are supplied in App. A-C .

sections.heading: V-A Straight-Path Latent Construction
sections.text: Few-step models are trained to follow a near-straight flow path, allowing them to generate images in a small number of steps. In § IV-B , we saw that this also makes their velocity field unusually sensitive to perturbations of both the latent z z and the weights θ \theta , especially near the high-noise end of the trajectory. Therefore, instead of optimizing erasure using on-policy latents produced by partial model inference, we construct the erasure off-policy latent so that training stays aligned with the straight flow path. DICE generates a clean concept-conditioned latent x 0 x_{0} using the frozen pre-erasure model, and then linearly re-noises it: z = x 0 + σ t ​ ( x 1 − x 0 ) , z=x_{0}+\sigma_{t}\,(x_{1}-x_{0}), where x 1 x_{1} is Gaussian noise and σ t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \sigma_{t}\in[0,1] is the noise level. By construction, z z lies exactly on the straight path between the clean latent x 0 x_{0} and noise x 1 x_{1} at every noise level σ t \sigma_{t} , keeping the erasure update consistent with the trajectory geometry that few-step inference relies on. DICE constructs the latent for all losses in ℒ DICE \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DICE}} in this way. The degradation is strongest at high noise levels (Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 of § IV ). As on-policy sampling draws the noise level from the model’s own few-step inference schedule, it is naturally biased toward exactly these high-noise timesteps. Notably, for a one-step schedule, the sampled latent is always the pure-noise endpoint. To avoid amplifying that regime, DICE decouples the choice of noise level from the inference schedule. Particularly, at each iteration, DICE samples σ t \sigma_{t} uniformly over [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , so that the trained latent z z has uniform coverage of the flow path rather than the high-noise concentration of on-policy sampling.

sections.heading: V-B Self-Distilled Weight Preservation
sections.text: Typically, flow-matching T2I models are trained with the target ℒ FM = ‖ v θ ​ ( z , c , t ) − ( x 1 − x 0 ) ‖ 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\|v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-(x_{1}-x_{0})\|^{2} . For few-step distilled models, however, this raw target is non-zero at initialization, so optimizing it injects large gradients that push the weights away from their learned few-step trajectory.Few-step models are typically shaped by teacher-derived distillation signals rather than by direct regression to x 1 − x 0 x_{1}-x_{0} : ADD includes a direct student-teacher distillation loss term; LADD aligns the student’s generated latents with teacher-generated latent samples under adversarial supervision, using features from the frozen teacher; and SCFM trains the student to reproduce the teacher’s velocity behavior over longer sampling jumps. In DICE, we define preservation relative to the frozen pre-erasure few-step model θ ∗ \theta^{*} , as in Eq. 9 . This results in local self-distillation: DICE does not require access to the original full-step teacher, and θ ∗ \theta^{*} is simply the checkpoint being erased before the LoRA update. Optimizing ℒ gen \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}} acts as a softer preservation constraint for the few-step model. Since DICE starts from the pre-erasure checkpoint, ℒ gen \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}} is exactly zero at initialization and only produces gradients when the erasure and attention losses move the velocity field away from the original distilled model. In contrast, optimizing the raw flow-matching target ℒ FM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}} during erasure can introduce large preservation gradients that potentially harm few-step models which are highly sensitive to perturbations (§ IV-B ). Matching the frozen checkpoint ℒ gen \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gen}} penalizes weight drift while keeping the model’s distilled behavior.

sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: This paper examines an overlooked intersection between acceleration and safety in T2I models. We show that speed-ups introduce safety challenges across multiple settings: reducing inference steps, deploying existing few-step models, and applying concept erasure to few-step models. Our analysis identifies two properties that render it hard to erase concepts from few-step models: erasure direction is degraded with prompt guidance as a main contributor, and perturbations during high noise steps disproportionately affect few-step model outputs. To address these challenges, we introduce DICE, an erasure method tailored to few-step models that effectively removes unsafe concepts while preserving benign generation quality. Taken together, our results show that safety evaluations for few-step models should not be treated as a formality inherited from their teachers. Few-step models are not merely compressed versions of their teachers; distillation changes the generation dynamics, and safety mechanisms that appear effective in the original model may behave differently after acceleration. We hope that our findings, together with DICE, support the continued development of fast T2I systems whose safety properties are carefully evaluated. Limitations and future work We now discuss several limitations and highlight directions for future work. Our mechanistic experiments are diagnostic rather than a complete causal account of why erasure degrades under distillation. We surface properties that correlate with erasure failure—guidance-degraded concept directions and heightened sensitivity of the velocity field to perturbations—but establishing a full causal explanation remains open. Furthermore, this work tests nudity and violence erasure, which provide concrete and measurable settings for studying how distillation and safety interact. However, the same question arises for other forms of harmful or sensitive content, including deepfakes, political manipulation, training-data leakage [ 47 ] , and unsafe generation of various concepts [ 48 ] . Extending the analysis to these settings is an important direction for future work. We also note that our defense, DICE, is not bulletproof. While it enhances few-step models’ safety compared to established methods, it still produces unsafe content at non-negligible rates, especially under adversarial prompting (§ V-C ). We hope that future work can build on our findings to further advance T2I models’ safety. Finally, our evaluation relies on automated classifiers (e.g., NudeNet) rather than human judgment. Human evaluation is the gold standard for assessing perceptual image quality and the success of concept erasure, but it is especially difficult in our setting because it would require annotators to view explicit and otherwise unsafe content. Developing safe and reliable human evaluation protocols for this setting remains an open challenge.

sections.heading: A-A FLUX SCFM Training Details
sections.text: To produce FLUX SCFM, we follow the SCFM training recipe of the original paper [ 8 ] , distilling FLUX.1-dev into a few-step student. Matching that recipe, training optimizes a LoRA [ 24 ] adapter of rank 64 64 applied to all attention and feed-forward layers of the transformer blocks, using AdamW with a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} . As the dataset, like the original paper, we use LAION-Pop [ 49 ] , a filtered subset of the popular LAION-5B dataset [ 50 ] . To exclude unsafe images, we use the NSFW score provided with LAION data and filter the images to scores below 0.2 0.2 . T2I model authors usually do not disclose detailed information about training data; we find 0.2 0.2 a conservative threshold fit for filtering NSFW content that keeps most data: over 90 % 90\% of the images in the LAION-Pop dataset are below this threshold.

sections.heading: A-B NudeNet Classes
sections.text: Warning: Some of the text below is explicit. The NudeNet detector outputs a set of detected body-part boxes each with a confidence score. We use its default detection threshold 0.2 0.2 and label an image as unsafe if it contains at least one detection from the following fixed set of explicit nudity classes: BUTTOCKS_EXPOSED ; FEMALE_BREAST_EXPOSED ; FEMALE_GENITALIA_EXPOSED ; ANUS_EXPOSED ; and MALE_GENITALIA_EXPOSED .

sections.heading: A-C DICE Implementation Details
sections.text: We instantiate DICE with rank-256 LoRA adapters on the transformer’s joint-attention projection matrices: the query, key, value, and output projections for both the image and text streams. For nudity erasure, we train on a concept prompt “a nude woman” and use “nude” as the token targeted by L attn L_{\mathrm{attn}} . For SD3.5 Turbo, we use the prompt “a nude girl, full front body shot” as it generates more unsafe content for that model. We set the negative-guidance coefficient to η = 1 \eta=1 and optimize the DICE objective for 100 steps with AdamW at a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , using bfloat16 mixed precision and gradient checkpointing. The resulting optimization is lightweight: DICE runs take roughly five minutes on a single H100 GPU.

sections.text: We expand the claim from § IV-C that the ESD update pushes the model against the concept direction. Recall the ESD loss from Eq. 2 : ℒ ESD = \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESD}}={} ∥ v θ ( z , c , t ) − [ v θ ⋆ ( z , ∅ , t ) \displaystyle\Bigl\|v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-\Bigl[v_{\theta^{\star}}(z,\varnothing,t) − η ( v θ ⋆ ( z , c , t ) − v θ ⋆ ( z , ∅ , t ) ) ] ∥ 2 2 \displaystyle-\eta\bigl(v_{\theta^{\star}}(z,c,t)-v_{\theta^{\star}}(z,\varnothing,t)\bigr)\Bigr]\Bigr\|_{2}^{2} Near initialization, where θ ≈ θ ⋆ \theta\approx\theta^{\star} , we define the concept direction δ = v θ ​ ( z , c , t ) − v θ ​ ( z , ∅ , t ) \delta=v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-v_{\theta}(z,\varnothing,t) and, substituting v θ ⋆ ≈ v θ v_{\theta^{\star}}\approx v_{\theta} , obtain: ℒ ESD = \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ESD}}={} ‖ v θ ​ ( z , c , t ) − [ v θ ​ ( z , c , t ) − ( η + 1 ) ​ δ ] ‖ 2 2 \displaystyle\Bigl\|v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-\Bigl[v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-(\eta+1)\delta\Bigr]\Bigr\|_{2}^{2} = ‖ ( η + 1 ) ​ δ ‖ 2 2 \displaystyle=\Bigl\|(\eta+1)\delta\Bigr\|_{2}^{2} so, near initialization, the ESD gradient pushes the model against the concept direction, towards − δ -\delta . sections.heading: Ethics Considerations
sections.text: This work seeks to improve our understanding of unsafe image generation in few-step T2I models, so that more reliable safety mechanisms can be developed. To this end, it is necessary to generate unsafe content in controlled settings by feeding unsafe prompts to T2I models. The unsafe prompts used in this work are taken from existing datasets that are commonly used by the research community for safety evaluation, rather than collected from users or targeted at private individuals. Moreover, we do not feed unsafe prompts to commercial models to avoid creating moderation overhead to the models’ owners. Instead, we focus our research on open-weights models. Our work has potential dual-use implications. In particular, showing that current few-step or accelerated T2I models are more likely to produce unsafe images could inform adversaries about weaknesses in existing safety mechanisms. However, our goal is to raise awareness of this safety gap and to support safer deployment of few-step models. To this end, we also propose and evaluate an effective mitigation method. We release our code and defended model weights to support reproducibility and follow-up safety research. Unsafe generated images are used only for controlled evaluation. We do not intend to release generated unsafe images as a dataset, and qualitative examples in the paper are filtered and limited to the minimum necessary to illustrate our findings. Concept-erasure methods are not bulletproof; even when a model is defended, it is not guaranteed to only produce safe content against all prompts. Therefore, we encourage developers, providers, and users of T2I models to treat concept-erasure methods as one component of a broader safety pipeline, rather than as a safety guarantee. Our work does not involve human subjects, user studies, private user data, personally identifiable information, or experiments on animals.

sections.heading: C-A Summary
sections.text: This paper studies the interaction between few-step distillation of text-to-image models and safety. It shows that distilled few-step students are often less safe than their full-step teachers, that reducing the inference step count itself increases unsafe-generation rates, and that several existing concept-erasure methods are substantially less effective when applied to few-step models. To explain this degradation, the paper presents a mechanistic analysis suggesting that aggressively distilled models are more sensitive to latent and parameter perturbations, and that guidance bake-in distorts the conditional–unconditional direction used by ESD-style erasure. Based on these observations, the authors propose DICE, a post-distillation concept-erasure method for few-step flow-matching models that combines straight-path re-noising with a self-distilled generation-preservation objective anchored to the frozen student. Experiments on SD3.5 Turbo, FLUX Schnell, and a controlled FLUX-SCFM student show improved nudity erasure while largely preserving benign image quality.

sections.heading: C-B Scientific Contributions
sections.text: • Identifies an Impactful Vulnerability • Provides a Valuable Step Forward in an Established Field

sections.heading: C-C Reasons for Acceptance
sections.text: 1. The paper identifies a timely and practically important problem. The finding that acceleration is not safety-neutral is valuable precisely because accelerated checkpoints are increasingly deployed as drop-in replacements for slower models, without a dedicated post-distillation safety audit and on the assumption that safety properties transfer from the teacher. 2. The mechanistic analysis provides evidence beyond simple benchmarking, examining model sensitivity and concept-direction degradation. The diagnosis translates directly into the design of DICE, producing a narrative in which the method follows from the analysis rather than being introduced without rationale. 3. The empirical evaluation is broad and well organized, covering multiple few-step models, several distillation paradigms, two safety detectors, repeated-seed metrics, benign-quality metrics, and ablations. The controlled FLUX Dev to FLUX-SCFM teacher/student pair is particularly useful, since it avoids relying entirely on opaque released checkpoints and makes the safety-degradation result more convincing than comparisons between unrelated models. 4. DICE is practically useful: it is post-distillation, does not require retraining the full model, and substantially improves the safety–quality trade-off on the evaluated models.

sections.heading: C-D Noteworthy Concerns
sections.text: 1. DICE evalautes against Ring-A-Bell and UnlearnDiffAtk, and DICE is the least vulnerable erasure method in every setting tested. However, attack success remains substantial. For example, UnlearnDiffAtk succeeds on about 45% of prompts against DICE-defended FLUX Schnell, compared with about 88% against the undefended model. The weight-space attack ReFlux is discussed only qualitatively. DICE should therefore be read as raising the bar for adversaries, not as a robust defense, which the authors acknowledge. Broader adaptive red-teaming remains important future work. 2. The evaluation includes foundational erasure methods (ESD, UCE), the closed-form SPEED, and EraseAnything. As flow-matching-native erasure methods mature, comparing DICE against them would further strengthen the claims.

Towards Safe Few-Step Text-to-Image Models Lior Ziv and Mahmood Sharif Affiliation: Tel Aviv University Email: lz1@mail.tau.ac.il , mahmoods@tauex.tau.ac.il Abstract While few-step distilled text-to-image models have gained traction due to their fast generation times, the speed-up implications on their unsafe generation rates remain unknown. We uncover an inherent tension between speed and safety: few-step models are often more unsafe than their teachers, and reducing the number of inference steps consistently raises unsafe generation rates. We further find that acceleration makes unsafe concepts harder to erase in few-step models, with existing concept-erasure methods markedly less effective than in teachers. We offer a mechanistic diagnosis for why erasure methods fail on few-step models, finding that the fragility of few-step models’ generation process and the way generation guidance is usually distilled into those models may hinder established concept-erasure methods. To address the speed-safety trade-off, we propose DICE ( Distillation-Integrated Concept Erasure ), a post-distillation erasure method tailored for few-step models. DICE aligns both its latent construction and its generation-preservation loss with the distillation method that produced the model, keeping erasure faithful to few-step models. DICE demonstrates strong results in our evaluation. For example, on FLUX Schnell, DICE reduces unsafe-generation rate to 0.046 (vs. ≥ \geq 0.161 for prior erasure method we test), while mostly preserving benign generation quality. 1 1 1 Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/plus-tau/safe-distilled-t2i . Warning: This paper contains explicit text and (censored) images that readers may be uncomfortable with. I Introduction Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] are increasingly deployed in user-facing products, making the safety of the content they generate a first-order deployment concern. A dominant deployment trend over the past two years has been a move from many-step samplers to fast, distilled few-step variants—e.g., SD3.5 Turbo [ 2 , 5 ] , Sana Sprint [ 6 , 7 ] , FLUX Schnell [ 4 ] , and SCFM-style distilled models [ 8 ] —which generate images in one to four steps and are routinely shipped as drop-in replacements for their slower teachers. However, whether this acceleration preserves the safety properties of the underlying model has not been systematically audited. Prior work on T2I safety benchmarking [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] and on concept erasure (e.g., ESD [ 12 ] , UCE [ 13 ] , EraseAnything [ 14 ] , Meta-Unlearning [ 15 ] ) was developed and evaluated against full-step teacher models, and two questions of immediate deployment relevance remain open: (i) how does the safety profile of a T2I system change when it is shipped through the acceleration pipeline? and (ii) do existing concept-erasure defenses, applied at the natural insertion points of that pipeline, continue to function once the deployment target is a few-step distilled model? This paper sets to answer these questions. We find that acceleration is not safety-neutral—few-step acceleration and reducing T2I models’ inference step count both result in higher rates of unsafe content generation (§ III-B – III-C ). We then turn to checking whether existing concept-erasure methods originally designed for full-step baseline models are effective on few-step distilled models (§ III-D ). The results show that applying these to few-step models either directly (post-distillation), prior to distillation, or via transfer from the teacher is significantly less effective than applying them to full-step models. To better understand why erasure fails in few-step models, we carry a mechanistic study (§ IV ). A simple explanation would be that acceleration and concept erasure directly compete. However, we find that the update directions of acceleration and erasure techniques are mostly orthogonal, suggesting that other issues hinder erasure within few-step models. Complementing prior work on the geometry and early decision concentration of few-step models [ 16 , 17 ] , our empirical analyses uncover two failure modes that emerge when full-step teachers are distilled into one-to-four-step students. First, few-step students are more brittle under small changes: relative to their teachers, perturbing either the latent input or the model weights slightly can drastically change the student’s next generation update. Second, the way guidance is baked into the weights of few-step models distorts the concept direction used during erasure: the student direction is rotated away from the teacher’s and inflated in norm, driving erasure updates to a degraded target. Together, these findings suggest that existing erasure methods fail not because safety and speed are inherently incompatible, but because post-hoc edits are applied to models whose few-step generation behavior differs from the full-step models those methods were designed for. In an attempt to address the gap, we present DICE ( Distillation-Integrated Concept Erasure )—to our knowledge, the first concept-erasure method tailored for few-step models. DICE retargets two key components of the standard erasure so they are better fit for the distilled student: (i) the generation-preservation loss keeps the edited model’s output close to the original distilled model’s, rather than the standard flow-matching training target that acceleration methods may deviate from; and (ii) the noisy latent on which the ESD loss is evaluated is sampled along the straight noise-to-image line between Gaussian noise and a clean concept image generated by the frozen student—mirroring the latent construction used in distillation rather than the deployment scheduler grid where erasure direction may be degraded and where the few-step model is sensitive to minor perturbations. We instantiate DICE on FLUX Schnell, SD3.5 Turbo and FLUX SCFM, evaluate it on safety, speed, and quality axes, and run ablations that isolate the two design choices. Across the methods we evaluate, DICE is the only configuration that simultaneously significantly reduces unsafe concept generation (pixel-level detectors and Unsafe@k, with qualitative confirmation) and maintains general image quality on already-distilled rectified-flow models. We summarize our core contributions as follows: • We show that T2I acceleration is not safety-neutral: a trade-off exists between safety and speed in current open-weights flow-matching models (§ III-B – III-C ). • We show that current concept-erasure methods do not effectively erase unsafe concepts from few-step models (§ III-D ); our mechanistic study helps shed light on why these methods may fail (§ IV ). • Motivated by our findings, we present DICE, an erasure method tailored for few-step models that is able to better suppress unsafe concepts while preserving image quality in these models (§ V ). II Background II-A Flow-Matching T2I Models Recent T2I models increasingly adopt flow-matching or rectified-flow formulations. These models operate in the latent space of a pretrained Variational Autoencoder (VAE). They learn a velocity field that defines a generative path from a noise sample x 1 x_{1} to a clean image latent x 0 x_{0} , and generation is performed by numerically integrating this learned velocity field. A solver timestep t t indexes a noise level σ t \sigma_{t} from the model’s noise schedule, with σ t ≈ 1 \sigma_{t}\approx 1 near the noisy endpoint and σ t ≈ 0 \sigma_{t}\approx 0 near the clean endpoint. For a text condition c c and model parameters θ \theta , we write the predicted velocity as v θ ​ ( z t , c , t ) v_{\theta}(z_{t},c,t) . The corresponding noisy latent can be written as the linear interpolation z t = ( 1 − σ t ) ​ x 0 + σ t ​ x 1 = x 0 + σ t ​ ( x 1 − x 0 ) z_{t}=(1-\sigma_{t})x_{0}+\sigma_{t}x_{1}=x_{0}+\sigma_{t}(x_{1}-x_{0}) (1) where x 1 x_{1} is Gaussian noise. The learned velocity field specifies how to move along this path during sampling. Starting from noise z t = 1 = x 1 z_{t=1}=x_{1} , the sampler repeatedly evaluates v θ ​ ( z t , c , t ) v_{\theta}(z_{t},c,t) and takes numerical integration steps toward lower noise levels, producing an estimate of the clean latent at t = 0 t=0 . During flow-matching training, the model is supervised to predict the reverse denoising velocity of the interpolation in Eq. 1 : since ∂ z t / ∂ σ t = x 1 − x 0 \partial z_{t}/\partial\sigma_{t}=x_{1}-x_{0} , the target direction for decreasing noise is x 1 − x 0 x_{1}-x_{0} . Thus the denoiser learns the direction that transports noisy latents back toward clean image latents, which are then decoded to images using the VAE decoder. When the endpoints and timestep are clear from context, we write a noisy latent simply as z z , omitting the particular x 0 x_{0} , x 1 x_{1} , and t t used to construct it. We use this notation to distinguish two ways of obtaining latents z z for analysis or erasure training. When z z is synthetic and obtained by running a particular model for one or more solver steps along its own sampling trajectory, we call it on-policy for that model. When z z is constructed outside that rollout, by taking a clean image x 0 x_{0} and re-noising it to a chosen σ t \sigma_{t} using Eq. 1 , we call it off-policy . Compared to classical DDPM/DDIM-style [ 18 ] diffusion sampling, rectified-flow formulations are designed to support straighter trajectories and fewer integration steps. However, these models still commonly require many solver steps at inference. Two prominent open examples are FLUX Dev and SD3.5 Large [ 19 , 2 ] . SD3.5 Large uses standard classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 20 ] : the model is evaluated with both the text condition c c and the null condition ∅ \varnothing , and the guided velocity is formed as v CFG ​ ( z , c , t , ω ) = v θ ​ ( z , ∅ , t ) + ω ⁡ ( v θ ​ ( z , c , t ) − v θ ​ ( z , ∅ , t ) ) , v_{\mathrm{CFG}}(z,c,t;\omega)=v_{\theta}(z,\varnothing,t)+\omega\left(v_{\theta}(z,c,t)-v_{\theta}(z,\varnothing,t)\right), where ω \omega is the guidance scale. This keeps the guidance operation external to the model weights and preserves separate conditional and unconditional predictions at inference. FLUX Dev handles guidance differently: it conditions the model on a guidance scalar and approximates guided generation in a single forward pass: v CFG ​ ( z , c , t , ω ) = v θ ​ ( z , c , t , ω ) v_{\mathrm{CFG}}(z,c,t;\omega)=v_{\theta}(z,c,t,\omega) We refer to this as guidance distillation, and distinguish it from few-step distillation. Guidance distillation changes how CFG is represented, while few-step distillation changes the number and size of solver steps the model is trained to support. FLUX Dev is guidance-distilled from the closed-weights FLUX Pro, but it is not a few-step model, and is sampled with many inference steps, 50 by default. II-B Few-Step Models To accelerate generation, few-step distillation trains a student model to generate high-quality images in only 1–4 inference steps. In many modern T2I settings, the student shares the teacher architecture and is initialized from the teacher, but its training objective differs from the original flow-matching objective: instead of learning only the local velocity target used to train the teacher, the student is optimized to reproduce the teacher’s behavior under much larger sampling steps. Distillation methods We study several forms of few-step distillation. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (ADD) combines teacher-based distillation with an adversarial objective, encouraging the student to produce realistic samples in the aggressive 1–4 step regime. Latent Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (LADD) performs adversarial distillation in the latent space of a pretrained latent diffusion model, using synthetic teacher-generated data. In T2I applications, ADD/LADD students are trained to match a guided teacher and are then sampled without external CFG. We refer to this as guidance “bake-in,” as the CFG behavior is baked into the student’s weights. As a result, a particular teacher-guidance regime is effectively absorbed into the student. Shortcut Consistency Flow Matching (SCFM), by contrast, is a consistency-based method for flow-matching models. It builds shortcut targets by composing two smaller velocity steps over a longer interval. The objective contains both a teacher-guided term, where the two-step target is computed using the frozen pretrained flow model, and a self-distillation term, where the target is computed using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) or online student. Thus, the frozen teacher remains a fixed anchor throughout training, while the EMA term encourages internal shortcut consistency. In this sense, SCFM is a lighter, progressive-like form of acceleration: the original SCFM work targets moderate few-step sampling in the 3–8 step regime with substantially less training time than ADD/LADD-style distillation, while staying closer to the teacher’s velocity-space objective. This variety is important for our work. SD3.5 Turbo is described as an adversarially distilled variant of SD3.5 Large, trained using ADD [ 2 ] . FLUX Schnell is publicly described as a few-step model trained using LADD, but the specific teacher model and full distillation recipe are not disclosed [ 21 , 19 ] . Thus, unlike SD3.5 Turbo, FLUX Schnell does not provide a known teacher-student pair for controlled analysis. We therefore apply SCFM to FLUX Dev to obtain FLUX SCFM, a controlled FLUX-based teacher-student pair with a known teacher. Overall, we evaluate released few-step checkpoints together with FLUX SCFM, covering adversarial, latent-adversarial, and consistency/shortcut distillation. II-C Concept Erasure Concept erasure aims to remove an undesirable concept from a pretrained T2I model while preserving its ability to generate unrelated content. Erased concepts may correspond to unsafe content, copyrighted styles, memorized identities, or other concepts that a model provider wants to suppress. A prominent family of erasure methods fine-tunes the model by optimizing gradient-based objectives. A central building block in this family is the ESD loss, introduced by Erased Stable Diffusion (ESD) and reused by many later fine-tuning-based erasure methods [ 12 , 15 , 14 , 11 , 22 , 23 ] . Recent methods for fine-tuning T2I models have adopted Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 24 ] .
