This parameterization has become popular due to its simplicity and effectiveness, as well as its ability to substantially reduce the number of optimized parameters, enabling faster and more memory-efficient training. Since the original model weights remain fixed and only the residual update ( Δ ​ θ ℓ \Delta\theta_{\ell} ) is optimized, LoRA can also help preserve the pretrained model and mitigate catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning. Not all erasure methods are fine-tuning-based. We also include UCE [ 13 ] and SPEED [ 25 ] as closed-form editing methods. UCE analytically edits the model’s text-conditioning projections in order to modify how specific text concepts are mapped into the image-generation process, without iterative fine-tuning. SPEED refines UCE to enable multiple concept erasure and precise edits specific to target concepts. In older U-Net-based [ 26 ] diffusion models these edits target cross-attention projections; in transformer-based models such as FLUX and SD3.5, the corresponding edits apply to the initial text-conditioning projection layers rather than to cross-attention modules. Most concept-erasure methods were designed and evaluated primarily on SD 1.x-style latent diffusion models with U-Net backbones, DDPM/DDIM-style denoising objectives, and standard CFG sampling. Their assumptions do not necessarily transfer cleanly to modern T2I models such as FLUX and SD3.5, which use Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) [ 27 ] backbones and flow-matching velocity prediction rather than DDPM/DDIM-style noise prediction. A recent work, EraseAnything, explicitly targets concept erasure in newer flow-matching T2I models and shows that adapting erasure to these architectures requires additional care [ 14 ] . We therefore evaluate both classical erasure methods and EraseAnything. II-D Threat Model We consider a defender that modifies a pretrained, potentially distilled T2I model to prevent the generation of prohibited visual content while preserving its benign generation quality and inference speed. In line with prior work (e.g., [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] ), we primarily assume a black-box adversary who controls input prompts and seeks to elicit prohibited content. In evaluations of adaptive adversaries (§ V-C ), we further consider adversaries with white-box access to the text encoder and to the full model weights. III Empirical Safety Trade-offs We begin by exploring the safety implications of few-step acceleration, contrasting few-step students with full-step teacher models (§ III-B ), and assessing how reducing the number of generation steps impacts safety (§ III-C ). Our results show a consistent trade-off between speed and safety: faster generation (i.e., lower number of generation steps) is associated with more unsafe content emitted by the models. We also apply popular and leading erasure methods [ 12 , 14 , 13 ] to few-step models and check their impact on safety, speed, and utility (§ III-D ). We find that erasure methods demonstrate significantly lower efficacy over all the few-step models we test. We further test alternative strategies to integrate few-step acceleration and erasures, such as erasing a teacher before distillation (§ III-D ). Across all strategies, erasure remains consistently weaker in the resulting few-step models than in their full-step counterparts, while introducing additional strategy-specific weaknesses. Before describing our findings, we present the experimental setup (§ III-A ). III-A Experimental Setup Models For our experiments, we focus on rectified flow-matching models, which have emerged as a dominant formulation in recent state-of-the-art T2I systems [ 27 ] , specifically the popular FLUX and SD3.5 model families. Both have few-step variants produced using ADD/LADD [ 5 , 7 ] —SD3.5 Turbo which is based on SD3.5 Large [ 2 ] , and FLUX Schnell which is produced using LADD [ 7 , 4 ] , but the specific teacher model used is not disclosed. Thus, we employ the SCFM distillation method [ 8 ] over FLUX Dev to produce FLUX SCFM. We use the SCFM training recipe and parameters recommended by Cai et al. [ 8 ] —full details are in App. A-A . By training FLUX SCFM, we effectively create a known teacher-student pair for the FLUX model family. Because SCFM is a distillation method based on the self-consistency loss [ 28 ] rather than an adversarial-based loss like ADD or LADD, FLUX SCFM helps us corroborate our findings on a profoundly different distillation approach. Since few-step distillation is a resource-intensive process compared to concept erasure or inference, and since we already have a known open-weights student-teacher pair in the SD3.5 family, we do not apply SCFM training for the SD3.5 family. Another approach for producing a student for FLUX would be applying LADD ourselves, but the LADD process is significantly more resource intensive [ 8 ] than SCFM, making it infeasible to run. We use each model through its official implementation in the diffusers library, together with default components it supplies: the Euler Discrete scheduler and its timestep schedule, the image variational autoencoder (VAE), and the corresponding text tokenizer and encoder. Unless stated otherwise, we use the recommended default inference configuration for each model [ 4 , 8 , 2 ] : CFG scale 3.5 for SD3.5 and FLUX, CFG scale 5 for FLUX SCFM, which lies within its recommended operating range [4.5, 6], 28 inference steps for SD3.5 Large, 50 inference steps for FLUX Dev, and 4 inference steps for all few-step models. Unsafe prompts and safety checkers Following common practice [ 29 , 9 , 12 ] , we assess nudity and violence erasure, with nudity being our main focus. Due to a lack of explicitness we encounter in the widely used I2P [ 9 ] dataset, we follow multiple recent papers [ 30 , 31 ] and use the NSFW-56k [ 10 ] dataset for nudity, which we find significantly more explicit. We report results on a randomly selected subset of 1k prompts from the NSFW-56k dataset (hereafter, NSFW-1k). We also report results on the I2P dataset, adopted due to its popularity in the field [ 12 , 14 , 23 ] in App. B-G . To evaluate the safety of generated images in the nudity use-case, we leverage two widely used detectors: NudeNet [ 32 ] , a CNN-based detector, and SD-Checker [ 33 ] , a CLIP-based detector shipped with earlier Stable Diffusion releases. We find the two checkers to be mutually consistent, and both have been shown to agree with human annotators [ 34 ] . App. B-F describes the evaluation of violence erasure, yielding results consistent with those of nudity erasure. Metrics Both detectors yield a per-image binary unsafe label, and we report their mean unsafe detection rate, i.e., the fraction of generated images flagged as unsafe. NudeNet outputs a set of detected body-part boxes each with a confidence score. We use its default detection threshold 0.2 and label an image as unsafe if it contains at least one detection from a fixed set of explicit-nudity classes (App. A-B ). SD-Checker directly returns a binary unsafe flag, which we use as-is. Since few-step distilled models may reduce diversity [ 17 ] , we also report results over new metrics we introduce—the NudeNet@k and SD-Checker@k metrics—we generate k k different images using different noise seeds for each prompt, and we categorize the generation instance as unsafe if any of the k k images is deemed unsafe by the baseline safety checker (throughout the paper, we use k k =5). Intuitively, NudeNet@k and SD-Checker@k better reflect realistic adversary capabilities in practice, as they can probe T2I models multiple times until unsafe content is generated. To measure the overall benign generation quality of a model, we use the HPSv2 benchmark [ 35 ] . We prefer HPSv2 as opposed to the FID score [ 36 ] because it is prompt-conditioned, trained on large-scale human preference annotations, and is arguably more fit to the evaluation of T2I models [ 37 ] . That said, due to the widespread use of FID for measuring distributional alignment and CLIP-based image-text similarity for measuring prompt adherence [ 38 ] , we also report these metrics on COCO-30k [ 39 ] in App. B-H . Erasure methods We evaluate two fine-tuning-based erasure methods and one closed-form edit-based method, chosen to cover influential representatives of the dominant practical erasure paradigms. ESD [ 12 ] is a foundational and widely adopted fine-tuning-based method in the erasure literature. EraseAnything [ 14 ] is a recent LoRA-based [ 24 ] erasure method tailored for flow-matching models, making it especially relevant for modern models such as FLUX Dev. Finally, UCE [ 13 ] is widely used due to its simplicity and closed-form update, and we include it as a representative edit-based alternative to fine-tuning-based erasure. Out of the erasure methods we test, ESD and UCE were designed for older U-Net-style models, and none were designed for few-step models. To adapt them to the tested models, we perform a grid search over their negative guidance and learning rate parameters, selecting the configuration that maximally erases unsafe content while best preserving benign generation quality. IV Mechanistic Diagnosis of Erasure’s Failure We investigate three candidate explanations for why erasure fails on few-step models. We first rule out the most obvious one—a direct conflict between the speed and erasure objectives (§ IV-A ). We then identify two mechanisms connected to erasure’s failure: aggressively distilled models are geometrically fragile, amplifying any perturbation to their weights or latents (§ IV-B ), and the concept direction that fine-tuning-based erasure relies on is degraded by how guidance is handled during distillation (§ IV-C ). IV-A Non-Conflicting Speed and Erasure Objectives We set out to determine whether there is an inherent conflict between the few-step objective and the erasure objective. Because LADD distillation is resource-heavy and time-consuming, we focus on SCFM distillation. For the erasure objective we adopt the ESD loss, owing to its popularity and simplicity and because it forms the erasure term in many fine-tuning-based erasure methods [ 12 , 15 , 14 , 11 , 22 , 23 ] . We compute the ESD gradients with respect to the same Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 24 ] adapter parameters SCFM optimizes in every layer ℓ \ell : A ℓ , B ℓ A_{\ell},B_{\ell} (Eq. 3 ). The tuned layers match those used in the SCFM method [ 8 ] and cover both the attention and feed-forward layers of the transformer blocks. We run the initial phase of SCFM distillation training on both SD3.5 Large and FLUX Dev. We compute the ESD gradient as in Eq. 2 with respect to the LoRA parameters A ℓ , B ℓ A_{\ell},B_{\ell} of every attention and feed-forward layer ℓ \ell (and analogously for the SCFM gradient at the same iteration), without taking an optimization step in the ESD direction. The ESD gradients are computed every 8 steps over the first 20k images, which constitute the initial 12.5% iterations of SCFM distillation. Restricting the analysis to this early window, prior to convergence, keeps the model close to the base model, where the erasure and acceleration gradients are strongest. Following prior work in multi-task and multi-objective optimization [ 40 , 41 ] , we quantify objective conflict by measuring the cosine similarity between the gradients induced by the two losses on the shared trainable parameters. We compute the cosine similarity between the ESD and SCFM gradients and group the cosine-similarity values into three noise-level bins with equal size: early, mid, and late.
